items.prompt: What does a manual check actually verify?
choices: That the code works correctly for every possible input, forever
One specific run, for the inputs tried, at the moment it was tried — it says nothing about other inputs or about whether it still works after a later change
That the code has no bugs anywhere in the codebase
The same thing an automated test verifies, just performed by a human
items.explanation: A manual check is a snapshot of one specific verification at one specific moment. It provides no ongoing guarantee — nothing about it re-runs automatically when unrelated code changes later, which is exactly the gap automated tests close.
items.reference:
📸 Manual check

one run, one moment, then permanently in the past

🔁 Automated test

the same check, re-runnable for free, forever

Why: a snapshot says nothing about tomorrow — only a repeatable check can.
items.learnMore:
A snapshot, not a guarantee

A manual check answers exactly one question: did this specific thing work, for these specific inputs, right now? It doesn't answer whether it will still work tomorrow, after code nobody thought was related changes underneath it. That gap — between 'worked when checked' and 'works' — is the entire argument for automated testing: the same check, made cheap enough to ask again and again.

This isn't a knock on manual checking as a first step — it's a limit on what it can prove about the future.

items.prompt: What specifically is a 'regression' in the sense this unit uses the word?
choices: Any bug present in the code from the very first version
Code that worked yesterday silently stopping working today because of an unrelated change elsewhere
A performance slowdown, specifically
A bug that only affects old browsers
items.explanation: A regression is specifically a break in previously-working behavior caused by a change somewhere else — the 'silently' and 'unrelated' parts are what make it hard for manual testing to catch: nobody knew to look there.
items.reference:
🕳️ Regression = worked yesterday, silently broken today, by a change that looked unrelated.

Why: manual testing only catches this if someone happens to re-check the exact thing that broke.
items.learnMore:
Why regressions are the hard case

A brand-new bug in code you just wrote is relatively easy to catch — you're already looking at that code. A regression is different: it's a break in something that already worked, caused by a change somewhere else that had no obvious connection. Catching it manually requires someone to correctly predict that the two are connected and go re-check the second thing — which gets less and less likely as a codebase grows and its web of dependencies gets harder to hold in one person's head.

This is exactly the problem automated tests are structurally suited to solve: they don't need anyone to predict the connection in the moment, only to have recorded it once.

Regressions and new bugs are the same thing, just different names
It was caused by a hardware failure, not a code change
items.explanation: The defining feature of a regression is present here exactly: previously-correct behavior (refunds handling fees over 100%) broke because of a change made somewhere else, for an unrelated reason, by someone with no visibility into the refund tool.

items.prompt: Which property means a test suite 'runs identically every time, not subject to a tired human skipping a step'?
choices: Speed
Repeatability
Specificity
Portability
items.explanation: Repeatability is exactly this: the same steps, run the same way, every single time, unaffected by fatigue, distraction, or memory — a property manual checking structurally can't guarantee.
items.reference:
🔁 Repeatability

same steps, every time

⚡ Speed

seconds, not hours

🎯 Specificity

names the exact break

Why: a manual check structurally can't guarantee any of these three.
items.learnMore:
The three properties

Repeatability, speed, and specificity are the three properties a good automated test has that a manual check structurally can't. Repeatability means the exact same steps run every time, unaffected by a human's memory or fatigue. Speed means a full suite can run in seconds, cheap enough to run before every single change rather than only before releases. Specificity means a failure names the exact assertion and file, rather than a vague 'something's broken.'

All three compound together: because it's fast, it gets run constantly; because it's repeatable, that constant running means something; because it's specific, a failure is immediately actionable.

items.prompt: What's the core trade being made when deciding whether to write an automated test?
choices: Upfront cost (writing the test now) for compounding savings (every future change gets checked against it for free, until the behavior deliberately changes)
There's no real trade — automated tests are strictly free to write and maintain
Test writing time versus how impressive the codebase looks to outsiders
The trade only exists for large companies, not individual developers
items.explanation: Writing a test costs real time once; not writing one costs nothing today but risks the same bug going undetected on every future touch of that code. The trade is upfront cost against compounding, ongoing savings.
items.reference:
💰 Pay once (write the test) → collect for free, every future change, forever.

Why: the trade only loses if the code is touched once and never again — rare in real systems.
items.learnMore:
Upfront cost vs. compounding savings

Writing a test costs real, one-time effort. What it buys in return isn't a single check — it's every future check against that same behavior, for free, for as long as the test exists. Not writing the test doesn't avoid the cost; it just defers it, and multiplies it, onto every future occasion someone has to rediscover, debug, and re-verify the same class of bug by hand.

The math only favors skipping the test when the code is genuinely touched once and never again — which is the exception, not the rule, in actively-developed systems.

items.prompt: Under what condition does the trade of 'write a test now' actually lose, according to this unit?

When the code is genuinely touched once and never again — the exception in most real, actively-developed systems, not the rule
Whenever the test would take more than 5 minutes to write
Whenever the codebase already has more than 100 tests
items.explanation: The compounding-savings argument depends on the code actually being touched again in the future. If it truly never is, the test never pays for itself — but real, actively-developed code is touched repeatedly, which is why that's the exception rather than the norm.

Scope of this unit

This unit deliberately stops short of teaching specific testing techniques — unit vs. integration vs. e2e levels, mocking strategies, coverage targets, and so on are each their own later units (see, for instance, testing-quality/test-pyramid for the level question specifically). What this unit establishes first is the underlying argument: why a manual check and an automated test make fundamentally different claims, and why that gap matters more, not less, as a codebase ages.

Technique choices without this foundation tend to become cargo-culted ('we write tests because that's what you do') rather than reasoned from the actual problem they solve.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does manual-only verification coverage tend to decay as a codebase grows, even if nobody decides to care less about quality?
choices: Developers become less skilled as codebases age

The cost of manually re-verifying everything stays roughly constant per check, while the number of things a given change could affect grows with the codebase — at some size, exhaustive manual re-checking becomes physically infeasible
Automated tests actively cause manual testing to be forgotten
Larger codebases have fewer bugs, so less checking is genuinely needed
items.explanation: This isn't a motivation problem — it's a scaling mismatch. As the codebase (and its web of dependencies) grows, the achievable manual-check coverage per unit of effort shrinks, and 'probably fine, didn't touch that file' becomes the de facto practice regardless of anyone's intentions.
items.reference:
📈 Codebase grows → 📏 cost per check stays flat → 🕳️ coverage as a % shrinks, on its own.

Why: nobody decided to check less carefully — the math of fixed cost vs. growing surface did it.
items.learnMore:
A fixed check against a growing surface

The mechanism is purely structural: re-verifying one change by hand costs roughly the same regardless of codebase size, but the number of places a change could ripple to grows as the codebase grows. At small scale, checking everything by hand is feasible. Past some size, it's mathematically impossible to keep doing within any real time budget — so coverage as a percentage of the whole system quietly shrinks, without anyone consciously choosing to test less.

This is why 'just be more careful' doesn't fix the underlying problem — the problem is the shape of the cost curve, not anyone's diligence.

items.prompt: In L2's `ship_change` pseudocode, what does `indirectly_affected` represent?
choices: Files the developer manually decided to skip out of laziness
Files that depend on the changed behavior but that the developer didn't know to check, because there's no way to know in advance which untouched files actually depend on it
Files that are always automatically safe from any change
A list the developer manually maintains of files never to test
items.explanation: `indirectly_affected` is exactly the set manual testing structurally can't cover reliably: dependents the developer has no visibility into at the time of the change, which is why the pseudocode routes it through `find_dependents` rather than the developer's own judgment.
items.reference:
directly_tested = what the developer thought to check.
indirectly_affected = what actually depends on it, known or not.

Why: an automated suite re-runs every existing check regardless of who remembers what depends on what.
items.learnMore:
Reading `ship_change`

The pseudocode splits a change's blast radius into two sets: directly_tested (what the developer manually checked, because they knew to) and indirectly_affected (everything that actually depends on the changed behavior, whether or not the developer knew it). The second set is exactly what a manual-only process can't reliably cover — it requires correctly predicting every place an effect propagates to, in a codebase no one person may fully hold in their head.

An automated suite doesn't need that prediction: it just re-runs whatever checks already exist, regardless of whether anyone remembered this file was affected today.

Three properties, compared directly

L2's table lines up manual checks against automated tests on the same three properties from L1: repeatability (memory-dependent vs. exact every time), speed (minutes-to-hours vs. often seconds), and specificity (vague symptoms vs. naming the exact assertion). items.learnMore:
Why speed compounds

Repeatability and specificity are properties of a single run of a check. Speed is different — it determines how many times that check actually gets performed. A check that costs seconds gets folded into every commit and every PR; a check that costs an hour gets reserved for releases, if it happens at all. The practical gap between 'constantly' and 'rarely' is exactly the window during which regressions can accumulate without anyone noticing, because the check simply wasn't run often enough to catch them close to when they were introduced.

A perfectly repeatable, perfectly specific check that only runs once a quarter still leaves a quarter's worth of undetected regressions.

choices: None — repeatability and specificity alone guarantee full protection regardless of how often it runs

A month's worth of regressions can accumulate undetected between runs, since the suite's other strengths don't matter if it isn't actually run often enough to catch them close to when they're introduced
The suite becomes less repeatable the less often it's run
6-hour test suites are impossible to write correctly
items.explanation: This is exactly L2's compounding-speed point: a check's other properties don't help if it isn't actually being run. Low frequency (driven by high cost) creates a real window where regressions pile up undetected, no matter how good the check is when it finally runs.
items.reference:
⚡ Cheap → run constantly. 🐢 Expensive → run rarely. The gap between them is where regressions accumulate.

Why: a check that isn't actually run provides zero protection, however good it is in principle.

items.prompt: Per L2's closing argument, what does NOT writing a test cost, compared to what writing one costs?
choices: Not writing a test costs literally nothing, ever — it's always the cheaper option

Writing a test costs real time once; not writing one costs nothing today but risks rediscovering, debugging, fixing, and re-verifying the same bug every future time the code path is touched, plus every regression going undetected until a manual re-check happens
Not writing a test costs exactly the same as writing one, just deferred
Writing a test is always more expensive in total than any number of future manual re-checks
items.explanation: L2's framing is specific: the test's cost is paid once, upfront. Skipping it doesn't eliminate cost — it converts a single upfront cost into a recurring, compounding one paid every time the code is touched again, plus the risk of undetected regressions in between.
items.reference:
✍️ Write once, pay once. 🔁 Skip it, and pay again — every future touch, potentially forever.

Why: the trade only loses if the code is genuinely touched once and never again.
items.learnMore:
The compounding cost of skipping a test

L2 closes by making the trade concrete: a test costs real time to write, once. Skipping it doesn't make that cost disappear — it just relocates the cost to every future occasion the same code path is touched: rediscovering the bug, debugging it, fixing it, re-verifying the fix by hand, and every future regression of the same bug going undetected until someone happens to manually re-check it.

The trade only loses when code is genuinely touched once and never again — which is the exception in real, actively-developed systems, not the rule.

Because testing is only worth it for code written by senior engineers
Because the math is actually identical for every single line of code, with no exceptions
Because 'most real code' is simply a rhetorical flourish with no actual reasoning behind it
items.explanation: The conclusion is conditional on the code being touched repeatedly — true for most real, actively-developed code, but not an absolute law, which is why L2 phrases it as 'most real code' rather than 'all code.'

items.prompt: A test asserts `expect(applyDiscount(100, 20)).toBe(applyDiscount(100, 20))`. Per L3's failure modes, what's wrong with this test?
choices: Nothing — it will always pass, which is the goal of a good test

It asserts the function's output equals itself, providing zero protection — a test's value comes from comparing against an independently-known-correct expected value, not from merely existing and passing trivially
It's testing the wrong function entirely
The syntax is invalid and won't run
items.explanation: A test that compares a function's output to itself can never fail, regardless of whether the function is correct or badly broken — it provides the appearance of test coverage with none of the actual protection, since there's no independently-correct expected value being checked against.
items.reference:
❌ expect(f(x)).toBe(f(x)) — always passes, proves nothing.

Why: a test's value comes from an independently-correct expected value, not from merely existing.
items.learnMore:
Assertions that prove nothing

A test's job is to compare a function's actual output against an independently-determined correct value. Comparing a function's output to a fresh call of the same function with the same arguments can never distinguish 'correct' from 'consistently wrong' — a badly broken implementation passes this test just as easily as a correct one.

This is a real trap, not a hypothetical one: it's easy to write when a developer is more focused on making a test 'pass' than on actually pinning down correct behavior.

items.prompt: What makes a test's expected value actually meaningful, per L3's first failure mode?
choices: That it was generated automatically by the test framework
That it's independently correct — determined some way other than just calling the function under test and using whatever it happens to return
That the test has a descriptive name
That the expected value is a round number
items.explanation: The entire point of an expected value is that it's known correct independently of the function under test. Deriving it by calling the function itself (as in the self-comparison example) removes exactly the property that makes the comparison meaningful.
items.reference:

items.prompt: A test asserts that `applyDiscount` internally calls a specific helper function, rather than checking its input/output behavior. What's the failure mode this illustrates?
choices: This is actually the best way to write a thorough test
Testing implementation details instead of behavior — the test breaks on every refactor even when the actual behavior is unchanged, training people to distrust or delete failing tests
There is no downside; this is equivalent to testing behavior
This only matters for functions with more than one helper
items.explanation: A test coupled to implementation details fails whenever the internals change, even if the observable behavior is identical — which teaches people that a red test doesn't necessarily mean something is actually broken, eroding the trust the whole practice depends on.
items.reference:
❌ Implementation

asserts a specific helper was called

✅ Behavior

asserts the actual input/output result

Why: behavior-focused tests survive refactors; implementation-focused ones don't.
items.learnMore:
Behavior, not implementation

A good test asserts what a function produces for given inputs, not how it produces it internally. Tests coupled to implementation details (which helper was called, what internal variable holds what value) break every time the code is refactored, even when nothing observable actually changed. This is corrosive over time: developers start treating red tests as noise rather than signal, and either ignore failures or delete tests rather than investigate them — exactly the opposite of what a trustworthy suite needs.

The fix is to test through the function's public contract (its inputs and outputs) and leave its internals free to change.

It makes the test suite run more slowly
It only affects tests written by less experienced engineers
items.explanation: The damage isn't just extra work fixing broken tests after a harmless refactor — it's that people learn a red test might be a false alarm, which is the same trust-erosion problem flaky tests cause, just from a different root cause.

items.prompt: Per L3, why are flaky tests (failing intermittently for reasons unrelated to actual correctness) described as particularly damaging, beyond just being annoying?
choices: They run slower than reliable tests, wasting CI time
They erode the trust the entire case for automated testing depends on — repeatability — training people to re-run failures until they pass rather than treating a failure as a real, meaningful signal
They only affect test suites larger than 1000 tests
They have no real downside beyond occasional false alarms
items.explanation: The core argument for automated testing rests on repeatability: the same check, run the same way, every time. A flaky test breaks that property directly — once people learn a failure might just be noise, they stop trusting failures at all, which defeats the entire mechanism this unit argues for.
items.reference:
🎭 A test people re-run until it passes isn't providing a signal anymore — it's theater.

Why: repeatability is the property flakiness destroys, and repeatability is the whole argument for testing.
items.learnMore:
Flakiness attacks the core premise

The entire case for automated testing, from L1 onward, rests on repeatability — the same check, run the same way, producing the same result every time. A flaky test (one that fails for reasons unrelated to real correctness, like timing assumptions or shared mutable state) directly contradicts that premise. Once a team learns that a given test's failure might just be noise, they stop trusting failures from it at all — and often start distrusting the suite more broadly.

A suite people habitually re-run until it goes green isn't providing a real signal anymore; it's providing the appearance of one.

items.prompt: A test occasionally fails because it depends on real network calls that sometimes time out, unrelated to the code being tested. What specific unit property does this undermine?

Repeatability — the test no longer runs identically every time in the sense that matters (a consistent, trustworthy verdict), even though the code under test hasn't changed
Specificity — the test now points at the wrong file
This has no connection to any of the unit's core properties
items.explanation: Repeatability isn't just about the steps being identical — it's about the check producing a trustworthy, consistent verdict. A test that sometimes fails for reasons having nothing to do with the code under test has lost exactly that property, even if its literal steps never change.

items.prompt: Per L3's fourth failure mode, does automated testing discover which behaviors matter on its own?
choices: Yes — automated tests automatically generate coverage for every important edge case
No — it makes a known-important behavior permanently checked once someone identifies it; it doesn't discover that behavior mattered in the first place
Yes, but only in codebases larger than a certain size
This question doesn't apply to automated testing at all
items.explanation: The refund tool's over-100% case only got a test because someone already knew it mattered. Automated testing locks in a known-important behavior so it stays checked forever — it doesn't independently go discover which behaviors are important in the first place.
items.reference:
🔍 Testing locks in what's already known to matter — it doesn't go find new things that matter on its own.

Why: testing pairs with understanding a function's full set of callers, it doesn't replace it.
items.learnMore:
Testing doesn't replace understanding

The `discountPercent: 150` case in L3 only became a test because someone already knew the refund tool depended on it. If nobody had ever noticed that dependency, no test would exist for it either — automated testing locks in protection for behaviors someone has already identified as important, it doesn't go looking for important behaviors on its own.

This is why testing pairs with, rather than replaces, the discipline of actually understanding a function's full set of callers before changing it — a comprehensive test suite still can't protect against a dependency nobody has ever identified.

items.prompt: Implement `applyDiscount(price, discountPercent)` from L3: it returns the price after applying the given percentage discount. It must correctly support `discountPercent` values above 100 (resulting in a negative price) — this is a real, intentional behavior the refund tool in L3 depends on, not a bug to clamp away.

tests.description: a 0% discount returns the original price
supports discountPercent above 100, producing a negative result (the refund tool's penalty case)

items.explanation: The correct implementation makes no assumption that discountPercent is capped at 100 — clamping it (as the well-intentioned 'fix' in L3 did) silently breaks the refund tool's legitimate use of values above 100. The last test here is exactly the regression test from L3: it exists specifically because that dependency was identified once and is now permanently checked.
items.reference:
❌ Clamped

silently breaks refunds' >100% case

✅ Unclamped

preserves both callers' real behavior

Why: a shared function's contract has to serve every real caller, not just the one you're currently looking at.
items.learnMore:
A shared function, two contracts

`applyDiscount` has exactly one job: subtract a percentage from a price. Checkout only ever calls it with values in [0, 100], but the refund tool legitimately calls it with values above 100 to model a penalty. 'Fixing' checkout's display of a bad discount by clamping the shared function silently changes the contract for every caller, not just the one the developer was looking at.

The right fix for checkout's bad-data problem lives at checkout's boundary (validate the input before it reaches the shared function), not inside the shared function itself.

items.prompt: Implement `supportsOverHundredDiscount(applyDiscountFn)`: given a discount function with the signature `(price, discountPercent) => number`, return `true` if it correctly preserves the refund tool's real behavior (i.e. `applyDiscountFn(100, 150)` equals `-50`), and `false` otherwise (e.g. if it clamps the discount and returns `0`). This is the same check that would have caught L3's regression before it shipped.

tests.description: returns true for the correct, unclamped implementation
returns false for the clamped 'fix' from L3

items.explanation: This is exactly the regression test from L3, restated as a reusable check: it verifies one specific, known-important behavior (the refund tool's over-100% case) regardless of which implementation is plugged in. This is what 'the dependency only needs to be identified once, and the suite remembers it forever' looks like in code.
items.reference:
🧪 One fact, checked forever: applyDiscount(100, 150) must equal -50.

Why: once a dependency is identified and written down as a test, no future developer needs to rediscover it.
items.learnMore:
Turning a known dependency into a permanent guard

The refund tool's dependency on discounts above 100% was, at some point, just something one developer happened to know. Writing it as a test converts that fragile, personal knowledge into a permanent, automatic check — any future change to `applyDiscount`, by anyone, gets validated against this fact without needing to already know it matters.

This is the practical mechanism behind L3's closing point: automated testing doesn't discover new important behaviors on its own, but it makes a known-important one permanently checked, which is exactly what would have caught the L3 regression before it shipped.

items.prompt: Implement `detectsClampRegression(applyDiscountFn)`: given a discount function `(price, discountPercent) => number`, return `true` if it exhibits the clamping bug from L3 (i.e. `applyDiscountFn(100, 150)` returns `0` instead of the correct `-50`), and `false` if it behaves correctly.

tests.description: returns false for the correct, unclamped implementation
returns true for the clamped 'fix' from L3

Either framing catches the exact same class of regression — what matters is that the known-important behavior is written down as an executable check at all.

items.prompt: Implement `regressionIntroduced(oldFn, newFn)`: given two discount functions with signature `(price, discountPercent) => number`, return `true` if `newFn` behaves differently from `oldFn` on the refund tool's known-important case (`price=100, discountPercent=150`), and `false` if they agree. This models what a test suite run before-and-after a change is really checking.

tests.description: returns false when the new version behaves the same as the old one
tests.expr: const correct = (p, d) => p - p * (d / 100); expect(regressionIntroduced(correct, correct)).toBe(false)

tests.description: returns true when the new version introduces the clamping regression
tests.expr: const correct = (p, d) => p - p * (d / 100); const clamped = (p, d) => p - p * (Math.min(d, 100) / 100); expect(regressionIntroduced(correct, clamped)).toBe(true)

items.explanation: This models the actual mechanics of a regression test: it doesn't need to know in advance what the 'right' answer is in the abstract — it just needs to confirm a known-important, previously-correct behavior hasn't silently changed. That's exactly what would have caught the checkout developer's 'fix' the moment it was run, before it ever reached production.
